title: Factorising Algebraic Expressions
description: Take out common factors and factorise linear expressions.

notes.heading: What is Factorising?

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the expression 3x + 6 rewritten as 3 times the bracket (x + 2).
illustration.caption: Factorising reverses expanding: the common factor 3 is pulled out of each term.

notes.body:
📌 Definition
Factorising is the process of rewriting an expression as a product of simpler expressions called factors.

🔑 Key Concept
Expanding multiplies a common factor into a bracket:
$$3(x + 2) = 3x + 6$$

Factorising does the opposite: it pulls the common factor back out:
$$3x + 6 = 3(x + 2)$$

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $4x + 8$.

Both terms are divisible by $4$:
$$4x + 8 = 4(x + 2)$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Factorising and expanding are inverse operations.
• The expression inside the bracket should have no further common factors.
• You can check by expanding the bracket again.

notes.heading: Highest Common Factor of Terms
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The highest common factor (HCF) of two or more terms is the largest factor that divides every term exactly.

🔑 Key Concept
To find the HCF of algebraic terms, look at two parts:
1. The HCF of the coefficients.
2. The common variables with the lowest power that appears.

💡 Worked Example
Find the HCF of $6x$ and $9x^2$.

Coefficients: HCF of $6$ and $9$ is $3$.
Variables: both terms contain $x$, and the lowest power is $x^1 = x$.
So the HCF is $3x$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Only take out factors that are present in every term.
• If a variable is missing from one term, it cannot be part of the HCF.
• Use the lowest power of each common variable.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Taking out a higher power than necessary. For $6x$ and $9x^2$, the HCF is $3x$, not $3x^2$, because $x^2$ does not divide $6x$ exactly.

notes.heading: Taking out a Common Factor
notes.body:
📌 Definition
To factorise by taking out a common factor, divide every term by the HCF and write the result inside a bracket with the HCF outside.

🔑 How it works
1. Identify the HCF of all terms.
2. Divide each term by the HCF.
3. Write the HCF outside a bracket containing the results.

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $5x + 10$.

Step 1: HCF of $5x$ and $10$ is $5$.
Step 2: Divide each term by $5$:
$$5x \div 5 = x \quad \text{and} \quad 10 \div 5 = 2$$

Step 3: Write the factorised form:
$$5x + 10 = 5(x + 2)$$

✅ Check
Expand: $5(x + 2) = 5x + 10$. This matches the original expression.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The number of terms inside the bracket equals the number in the original expression.
• The sign of each term inside the bracket must be correct.
• Always check your answer by expanding.

notes.heading: Factorising Linear Expressions
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A linear expression in one variable has the form $ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are numbers. Factorising it means writing it as a single common factor multiplied by a bracket.

🔑 How it works
Look for the HCF of the coefficient and the constant term, then write:
$$ax + b = c\left(\dfrac{a}{c}x + \dfrac{b}{c}\right)$$
where $c$ is the HCF.

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $7x + 14$.

The HCF of $7$ and $14$ is $7$:
$$7x + 14 = 7(x + 2)$$

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $12x - 18$.

The HCF of $12$ and $18$ is $6$:
$$12x - 18 = 6(2x - 3)$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Leaving a common factor behind, such as writing $12x - 18 = 2(6x - 9)$. This is not fully factorised because $6x - 9$ still has a common factor of $3$.

notes.heading: Factorising with Algebraic Common Factors
notes.body:
📌 Definition
When every term contains the same variable, that variable is part of the common factor.

🔑 How it works
Take out both the numerical HCF and the common variable raised to its lowest power.

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $x^2 + 5x$.

Both terms contain $x$. The lowest power is $x^1 = x$.
Divide each term by $x$:
$$x^2 \div x = x \quad \text{and} \quad 5x \div x = 5$$
So:
$$x^2 + 5x = x(x + 5)$$

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $8xy - 12x$.

Numerical HCF of $8$ and $12$ is $4$.
Common variable: $x$.
Divide each term by $4x$:
$$8xy \div 4x = 2y \quad \text{and} \quad -12x \div 4x = -3$$
So:
$$8xy - 12x = 4x(2y - 3)$$

✅ Check
Expand: $4x(2y - 3) = 8xy - 12x$. Correct.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• If one term has no variable, you cannot take that variable out of every term.
• Take the lowest power of each common variable.

notes.heading: Factorising Expressions with Negative Terms
notes.body:
📌 Definition
When the leading term is negative, it is often neatest to take out a negative common factor so that the first term inside the bracket becomes positive.

🔑 How it works
A negative common factor changes the sign of every term inside the bracket.

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $-6x + 15$.

The HCF of $6$ and $15$ is $3$. Take out $-3$:
$$-6x + 15 = -3(2x - 5)$$

Check by expanding:
$$-3(2x - 5) = -6x + 15$$

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $-10x - 20$.

Take out $-10$:
$$-10x - 20 = -10(x + 2)$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to change signs when taking out a negative factor. If you write $-6x + 15 = -3(2x + 5)$, expanding gives $-6x - 15$, which is wrong.

notes.heading: Checking and Presenting Your Answer
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A fully factorised expression has no common factor left to remove from the terms inside the bracket.

🔑 How it works
1. Factorise completely.
2. Expand your answer mentally or on paper.
3. Compare with the original expression.

💡 Worked Example
Factorise $9x^2 + 15x$ completely.

Numerical HCF of $9$ and $15$ is $3$.
Common variable factor is $x$ (lowest power).
Take out $3x$:
$$9x^2 + 15x = 3x(3x + 5)$$

Check: $3x(3x + 5) = 9x^2 + 15x$. Correct.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always write the simplest possible bracket contents.
• Check that the terms inside the bracket have no further common numerical or algebraic factor.
• It is good practice to expand your final answer to verify.

✅ Check
For $18x - 24$, taking out $6$ gives $6(3x - 4)$. The bracket $3x - 4$ has no common factor, so the answer is fully factorised.

flashcards.definition: To rewrite an expression as a product of simpler expressions called factors.
A factor that divides every term in an expression exactly.
flashcards.example: $5$ is a common factor of $5x$ and $10$.

flashcards.definition: The largest factor shared by every term in an expression.
An expression of the form $ax + b$ where the variable has power $1$.

flashcards.term: Factorising by taking out a common factor
flashcards.definition: Divide every term by the HCF and write the result inside a bracket.
Factorising undoes expanding because both produce equivalent expressions.
A variable or power that appears in every term of the expression.

flashcards.term: Lowest power of a common variable
flashcards.definition: When taking out a variable, use the smallest exponent that appears in all terms.
flashcards.example: For $x^3 + x^2$, take out $x^2$ to get $x^2(x + 1)$.

flashcards.definition: Taking out a negative factor so that the leading term inside the bracket becomes positive.
An expression is fully factorised when the terms inside the bracket share no further common factor.
flashcards.example: $6x + 9$ is fully factorised as $3(2x + 3)$; the bracket $2x + 3$ has no further common factor.

flashcards.definition: A method to verify factorisation by multiplying the common factor back into the bracket.
A term with no variable part, which may still share a numerical common factor.
flashcards.example: In $6x + 15$, the constant term is $15$ and the HCF is $3$.

questions.explanation: The HCF of $3x$ and $9$ is $3$. Dividing each term by $3$ gives $x + 3$, so $3x + 9 = 3(x + 3)$.
The HCF is $5$. $5x \div 5 = x$ and $-15 \div 5 = -3$, so $5x - 15 = 5(x - 3)$.
The HCF of $8$ and $12$ is $4$. Dividing gives $2x + 3$, so $8x + 12 = 4(2x + 3)$. The bracket $2x + 3$ has no further common factor.
The common factor is $x$. $x^2 \div x = x$ and $4x \div x = 4$, so $x^2 + 4x = x(x + 4)$.
The HCF is $7$. $7x \div 7 = x$ and $-21 \div 7 = -3$, so the answer is $7(x - 3)$.
The HCF of $6$ and $10$ is $2$. Dividing gives $3x + 5$, so $6x + 10 = 2(3x + 5)$.
The HCF is $9$. $9x \div 9 = x$ and $-18 \div 9 = -2$, so $9x - 18 = 9(x - 2)$. Option $3(3x - 6)$ is not fully factorised.
The common factor is $x$. $xy \div x = y$ and $3x \div x = 3$, so $xy + 3x = x(y + 3)$.
Taking out $-4$ gives $-4(x - 3)$ because $-4x \div (-4) = x$ and $12 \div (-4) = -3$. Expanding confirms: $-4(x - 3) = -4x + 12$.
The HCF of $10$ and $25$ is $5$. Dividing gives $2x + 5$, so $10x + 25 = 5(2x + 5)$.
The HCF of $12$ and $8$ is $4$. $12x \div 4 = 3x$ and $-8 \div 4 = -2$, so $12x - 8 = 4(3x - 2)$. The bracket cannot be factorised further.
The common factor is $x$. $x^2 \div x = x$ and $6x \div x = 6$, so $x^2 + 6x = x(x + 6)$.
Taking out $-5$ gives $-5(x + 4)$ because $-5x \div (-5) = x$ and $-20 \div (-5) = 4$. Expanding gives $-5x - 20$, matching the original.
The HCF of $15$ and $35$ is $5$. Dividing gives $3x + 7$, which has no further common factor, so $15x + 35 = 5(3x + 7)$.
The HCF is $2x$. $4xy \div 2x = 2y$ and $-10x \div 2x = -5$, so $4xy - 10x = 2x(2y - 5)$. The other options are not fully factorised or incorrect.
